newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian leaders fight final battle of campaign.
newsitem.headline: Canadian leaders fight final battle of campaign.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien and his rivals had their final chance before Canada's federal election to face each other on Sunday night, but the truncated debate was so short that it proved impossible to score knock-out punches.
The leaders had agreed to debate the question of Quebec sovereignty in French for 42 minutes to finish up a debate on Tuesday that had been cut short when the moderator fainted.
"I found the debate a little short today. We didn't get time to get warmed up," Chretien told reporters afterward.

Chretien, fighting for re-election nationally while struggling to build Liberal Party popularity in his native Quebec, called the June 2 election 1-1/2 years before he had to in order to cash in on a strong national lead in the polls.

A spate of surveys since an English debate on Monday and the partial debate on Tuesday showed Conservative Party leader Jean Charest surging ahead and separatist Bloc Quebecois leader Gilles Duceppe losing ground.
Duceppe aimed to make a strong impression to rescue his flagging campaign, Charest was hoping to build on his momentum and Chretien needed to appear that he was doing more than just avoiding damage.

Duceppe did declare clearly his intention to push for Quebec independence: "I'm calling on all Quebeckers and all those who believe Quebec must be stronger to join your voices to ours to say who we are, to say who we want to be, to say we are our own country, Quebec."
But after accounting for opening and closing statements, only 28 or 29 minutes was left for debate and there was little of the cut-and-thrust argumentation that characterized the earlier debates.
"It didn't help me make my mind up at all," a woman in the audience in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation studio, Claude Berthiaume, told Reuters afterward.
Only two of the audience of about 20 said they had changed their mind because of the debates, both of them opting for Charest.
One, Patrick Aubin of Montreal, said he voted for the Bloc in the 1993 elections but was attracted by the 38-year-old Charest's "vibrant spirit, his youthful vision, his dynamism." Chretien is 63.
The other party leaders were the right-wing Reform Party's Preston Manning and the leftist New Democratic Party's Alexa McDonough.

McDonough said Chretien needed to worry more about the economy, charging that the reason his own electoral district voted in favor of Quebec sovereignty in a hotly contested referendum in October 1995 was because of the 16 percent level of unemployment.

Manning, only running candidates in a handful of Quebec seats, used the debate to bring his tough-love message that shows the real cost of potential separation, while also advocating giving all provinces including Quebec more power.
He said it was important to declare that if Canada was divisible, so was Quebec -- a thought designed to make separatists uncomfortable.

A few in the audience, mainly from Quebec, said they thought the Reform leader had new ideas. Manning freely admits he is unlikely to win seats there this time, but he hopes his message will resonate with voters outside the province.

One of the problems faced by those trying to keep Canada from falling apart is that the separatists are allowed to keep coming back again and again until they win -- although support at the moment seems to be on the wane.
"Mr. Duceppe was unable to answer when I asked him, 'When will you accept democracy in Quebec?'" Chretien said afterwards.

"It's necessary to turn the page, to work on real problems, problems of Quebeckers and other Canadians -- jobs, health care, maintaing the social safety net, youth, the presence of Canada in the world, the participation of Canada and Quebec in the Pacific."
